title: Your giving
tomorrow: what does Shabbat smell like as it leaves?

lines: SIGN IT, OR KEEP IT SECRET?
cards: Donation pages show a running list: names, amounts, little hearts. Some people tick the box for anonymous. Some put their name in bold so friends will match it.
Noa is giving her summer job money to the hospice that cared for Owen's grandma. Owen says sign it, so others give. Saba says keep it secret.
Both of them have Jewish sources on their side.

teach.b: Saba's side first. Proverbs says "A gift in secret pacifieth anger."
The Talmud praises giving in secret, and Maimonides, laying out the levels of tzedakah, ranks high the gift where the giver and the one receiving don't know each other.
Its strongest case: no one is shamed, and the giver isn't buying a reputation. Now Owen's side.

The Rema, whose notes on Jewish law are printed with the Shulchan Aruch, writes that someone who gives to tzedakah may have their name written on the gift, as a memorial, and that it's fitting to do so.
Its strongest case: a name can move others to give, and a gift in someone's memory can carry their name forward. Both sides agree on the main thing.
Tzedakah isn't extra credit; it's owed. And over time it finds a home: a hospice, a food pantry, a school, a cause you keep coming back to.
That's your cause. Something to tell a friend tonight: Jewish law has room for a secret gift and for a name on the plaque.

how: Jewish giving, tzedakah, is treated as a duty; some give anonymously, some dedicate gifts in a loved one's name, and some synagogues list donors or put names on plaques in memory.

o: a club you joined to meet new people
a single gift you give once to feel good
the need you choose to keep giving to

games.q: two ways to give — tap the pairs.
p: a name on the gift, as a memorial

s: Jewish law forbids putting your name on a gift
the Rema says a giver may write their name on it as a memorial.
Maimonides ranks high a gift where giver and receiver don't know each other
no one is shamed, and no one is buying a name.
in Jewish teaching, tzedakah is extra credit, beyond what's required

games.q: you're giving to a friend's fundraiser. the page lets you show your name or stay anonymous. what's the strongest case for showing your name?
o: it can move others to give, and a name can be a memorial.
people ought to know who the generous ones are.
a gift without a name doesn't really count as much.
games.why: the Rema allows a name as a memorial, and a name can move others. the other side is strong too: Maimonides prizes a gift where neither side knows the other. both are Jewish positions.

practice: Choose the cause that's become yours, the one you keep coming back to. Give something to it now, even a small amount, and decide as you do: your name on it, or no name at all.

wordCard.voice: Your giving: tzedakah that finds a home, the cause you return to, given in secret or with your name on it.

orig.note: Hebrew: the word Jews use for giving to those in need.
